name: Hassan Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the cold store at a frozen food depot. We supply restaurants, school kitchens and hospitals, so it's chips, peas, fish fillets, boxes of ice cream. Inside it's minus twenty-five, so you wear a thick suit and gloves, and you come out every ninety minutes to warm up. I'm on lates, two till ten.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work, and the old boys in there look after you. My father drove lorries for thirty years and he always said, a man who works with his hands never goes hungry. What wears me out is the cold in my fingers, and the scanner. It freezes, it logs me out, and then the team leader, Steve, says my numbers are down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I knew it, it was all talk from people who've never done a day's lifting. At work everyone would agree with me. I'm not on social media much, so that's where it'd stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes for me, and that's fine, but I've still got plenty on my plate. Minus twenty-five in the freezer and the wedding hall wants a deposit by March, and neither of those cares about AI. Sara, my fiancée, and I have about two months of bills saved, plus a separate pot for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, take any extra shifts in the run-up to Christmas, and keep feeding the wedding pot. I'd try to get my numbers up so Steve stops talking to me about them. That's it, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled about AI, tense about money. The wedding is a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if your numbers stay down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think they'd sack me, the cold store is hard to staff. But they could move me to ambient, the normal warehouse, which means losing the cold allowance. That's about forty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does Sara work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She works at a dentist's reception. She's better with computers than me, she does the bookings on a system. She keeps telling me to try the AI thing on my phone, and I keep saying no.

say: I'd say AI was **all talk** from people who never lifted anything.
I'd say it at **work**, not online.
think: AI isn't my worry; the **wedding deposit** due in March is.
We have about **two months** of bills saved plus a wedding pot.
do: Take **extra Christmas shifts** and keep feeding the wedding pot.
Try to **raise my pick numbers** so the team leader backs off.
feel: **Settled** about AI but **tense** about wedding costs.
S0.quote: Minus twenty-five in the freezer and the wedding hall wants a deposit by March, and neither of those cares about AI.
fieldNote: His pressure in a plateau is the **wedding**, not technology.
Losing the **cold allowance** of about forty a week is a real risk.
He **refuses AI** even though his fiancée Sara uses it at work.

steps.text: Take extra cold store shifts before Christmas
Pay into the wedding pot every payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say machines are fine for the office, but you need men on the floor. At work I'd say it, and at the mosque on Friday with the older men. I don't think the government should be paying people to sit at home either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office would change first, the people who plan the routes and book the lorries. But I'm not stupid about the cold store. Nobody wants to stand in a freezer for eight hours, so the freezer is exactly where the company will put robots first. They've already built one automatic freezer at the depot up north.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working hard and keep my head down. I'd cut the wedding guest list from two hundred to a hundred and fifty to save a bit. And I'd talk to my uncle, who runs a tyre-fitting garage, just to know the door is open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Like there's a draught coming under the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government shouldn't pay people to sit at home. What if it's you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to work, not take a handout. If the company brings in robots, they should train their own men to run them, like an apprenticeship. That's fair, that's not charity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your father?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say keep going and don't complain. But he'd also know, he saw lorries get trackers and cameras, and half his mates left. He'd tell me to listen to my uncle.

say: I'd say **machines** suit the office, but you need men on the **floor**.
I'd say government shouldn't **pay people** to sit at home.
think: Office route planning and booking go to **AI** first.
The **freezer** is where robots go first, and one depot already has one.
do: Cut the **wedding guest list** from two hundred to one hundred and fifty.
Ask my uncle if his **tyre garage** would take me on.
feel: **Worried**, like a draught coming under the door.
S1.quote: Nobody wants to stand in a freezer for eight hours, so the freezer is exactly where the company will put robots first.
fieldNote: He sees the **cold store** as a prime robot target, despite his public stance.
His **uncle's garage** is his quiet fallback.

steps.text: Cut the wedding guest list to one hundred and fifty
Ask his uncle about work at the tyre garage
Keep working lates in the cold store

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is people in fancy offices playing with things they don't understand. I'd say families and communities will have to hold together, because the government won't save us. At the mosque we'd be talking about nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the AI, and the office is gone. By 2031 there's a robot in the freezer and I'm out, maybe with a baby on the way by then. I'm not good with screens, so I don't see what job I'd move to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd swallow my pride and ask my uncle for a job at his tyre garage, because family looks after family. I'd postpone the big wedding and do a small one at the mosque hall. Every pound saved would go into the account, aiming for six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd feel like I was letting Sara down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't tyre fitting be hit by robots too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but every car is different, rusty bolts, wrong sizes. My uncle's had the same customers for twenty years. People trust a face they know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sara say about a smaller wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be upset, then she'd be practical, she always is. Her mother would be the problem. But a big wedding and no job is worse than a small wedding and a job.

say: I'd blame **people in offices** playing with things they don't understand.
I'd say **families and communities** must hold together, not wait for government.
think: By **2031** a robot takes the freezer and I'm out.
I'm **bad with screens**, so I can't see the next job.
do: Ask my uncle for work at his **tyre garage**.
Swap the big wedding for a **small one** at the mosque hall.
Save every spare pound towards **six months** of bills.
S2.quote: I'd swallow my pride and ask my uncle for a job at his tyre garage, because family looks after family.
fieldNote: His answer is **family**, not the state.
A **small wedding** becomes a practical sacrifice.
He fears **letting down** his fiancée more than losing the job.

steps.text: Ask his uncle for a job at the tyre garage
Hold a small wedding at the mosque hall instead
Save every spare pound towards six months of bills
Lean on his uncle and father for help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should be enough for companies to train their own people, if they've got any decency. I'd say it at work. I'd vote for whoever talks about apprenticeships, not benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI by 2031, robots in the freezer by about 2034. By then I'd probably have a child. I'd want my children to see their father go to work every morning, not sit at home waiting for a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the wedding as planned but keep it smaller. I'd go to my uncle's garage on Saturdays to learn tyre fitting, unpaid if needed. I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like carrying a box that's slowly getting heavier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're slow with new things. Would Saturdays at the garage be hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but it's spanners, not screens. I can learn with my hands. It's the computers that make me feel stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What keeps you up at night in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The year 2034. That's when we'd want a second child, maybe a bigger flat. And that's when the freezer gets its robot.

say: I'd say companies should **train their own people** with five years' notice.
think: Robots reach the freezer by about **2034**, when I'd likely have a child.
I want my children to see me **go to work**, not wait for a cheque.
do: Learn **tyre fitting** at my uncle's garage on Saturdays.
feel: **Heavy**, like a box slowly getting heavier.
S3.quote: I'd want my children to see their father go to work every morning, not sit at home waiting for a cheque.
fieldNote: Robot timing collides with **family plans** around 2034.
He can learn **with his hands** but fears screens.
His politics favour **apprenticeships** and company training over welfare payments.

steps.text: Learn tyre fitting at his uncle's garage on Saturdays
Hold a smaller wedding than planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off and a lot can change. Maybe the robots never work in the cold. At work I'd say don't worry about it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I'll have a wife, maybe two kids, and a robot will turn up just when they need shoes. So I can't fully relax. But it's far enough that I'd focus on the wedding and the flat first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, nothing big. Have the wedding, keep working lates, keep saving. Maybe start helping at my uncle's garage now and then, just to keep the door open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. Some worry in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the robot freezer up north working properly and they started talking about one for us. Then I'd go to the garage properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try the AI on your phone, like Sara says?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if she sat with me. I'm not against it for her. I just don't see what it does for a man picking frozen peas.

say: I'd say it's **a long way off** and robots may never work in the cold.
I'd tell colleagues **not to worry** yet.
think: Robots could arrive just as **my kids** need shoes.
It's far enough to focus on the **wedding and flat** first.
do: Hold the **wedding** and keep working lates.
Help at my uncle's **garage** now and then to keep the door open.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with **worry** at the back of his mind.
S4.quote: In ten years I'll have a wife, maybe two kids, and a robot will turn up just when they need shoes.
fieldNote: A decade lets him put **family first** for now.
His **trigger** is the automatic freezer at the northern depot spreading.
He might try AI only with **his fiancée's** help.

steps.text: Go ahead with the wedding next summer
Keep working lates in the cold store
Help at the uncle's tyre garage now and then

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have no time and I'm not good at changing. What would help is companies training their own workers on the new machines, like a proper apprenticeship, and family close by.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what work means to people like me. Work is how a man shows his family he's worth something. Take the work away and you have to give him something else to do, not just money.

headlineQuote: Work is how a man shows his family he's worth something. Take the work away and you have to give him something else to do, not just money.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old cold store picker** at a frozen food depot, engaged to Sara and saving for the wedding.
He is **traditional**, values hard work and family, and wants apprenticeships rather than handouts.
He **avoids AI** and screens but knows the freezer is a likely first place for robots.
His fallback is his **uncle's tyre garage**, and family is his safety net.
His mood runs from **uneasy** in slow scenarios to **alarmed** when robots arrive by 2031 or 2034.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no time and struggles with change.
whatWouldHelp: Company-run **apprenticeships** on the new machines and **family** close by.
